USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 lists in place, including the already-announced January 1, 2019 step-up of List 3 from 10% to 25% as unspent leverage, and use the scheduled Trump–Xi meeting at the G-20 to test whether Beijing will put a serious, verifiable offer on IP, forced tech transfer, and market access. Do not add a new $267B tranche before that meeting, and do not trade away tariffs for another vague purchase pledge of the May 19 type. If China arrives empty-handed, the January hike can proceed without a new decision; if it arrives with structural concessions, delay or narrow that hike in exchange — do not pre-commit.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a modest US opportunity, not an existential hit. The 301 record and the cascade from the March 22 memorandum through List 3 on September 24 put roughly $250B of Chinese imports under tariff, while China’s matching goods retaliation is smaller and already exhausted its proportional tariff space (US goods exports to China are far smaller than US imports). China is showing more strain than the US real economy: industrial production slowed from 6.8% to 5.9% y/y, FX reserves fell about $56B over the window, and CNY weakened to 6.93 (about +9.7% USD). US consumer sentiment remains high (98.6), industrial production is still above spring levels, and the administration has publicly treated US growth versus a Chinese slowdown as bargaining terrain. That is why the score sits near the opportunity side of zero, not at the +0.5 “material GDP drag” anchor.

The score is only mildly negative because the costs are already visible and the “easy win” claim is not holding. US goods exports to China have fallen about 11.6% over the window (to $9.2B) while imports from China have risen about 18.7% (to $52.1B) as buyers front-run tariffs, and the goods trade deficit has widened to −$76.5B. China has targeted soybeans and other farm goods — a $12–14B market and the heart of US ag surplus with China — just as the US harvest window opens. VIX jumped to 24.98 on October 11 in a broader rates-and-trade selloff, and Baa yields have pushed above 5%. A further unilateral escalation into the remaining ~$267B (more consumer goods) before G-20 would raise US household and supply-chain costs without a new Chinese structural offer, and might harden Beijing rather than extract one. August talks produced no movement; the May 19 “significantly increase purchases” statement collapsed within ten days. That history argues for talks without new US commitments, not for rollback or another purchase-only deal.
key_factors: US has unused leverage: $250B already covered; List 3 10%→25% set for Jan 1 2019; remaining ~$267B still threatened
China showing more macro stress (IP slowdown, reserve decline, CNY ~6.93) than the still-firm US real economy
US export pain is concentrated and real: EXPCH -11.6%, soy/farm retaliation into harvest, goods deficit worse because imports are being front-run
G-20 Trump–Xi meeting is the first leader-level opening since August; August working-level talks went nowhere
May 19 purchase-truce collapsed by May 29 — do not repeat a goods-only deal that leaves 301 structural issues unaddressed

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current retaliatory posture and do not add new tariffs, non-tariff strikes, purchase commitments, or a break of 7 on the yuan. Keep a quiet channel open, but offer no structural concessions while Washington is demanding what looks like surrender and still has a $267B follow-on list ready. Use domestic liquidity and fiscal support already underway to absorb the shock, and revisit talks only if the United States signals a willingness to pause the January 1 step-up to 25%.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. Combined Section 301 coverage is now about $250B of Chinese exports after List 3 took effect at 10% on 24 September, with that rate scheduled to rise to 25% on 1 January 2019, and Trump has already threatened a further ~$267B that would cover essentially all remaining shipments to the United States. That is a material hit to the export model and to Made in China 2025 sectors first targeted on the $50B lists, amplified by the 16 April ZTE denial order as a demonstrated firm-level kill switch. Macro stress is real: CNY has weakened from about 6.32 in late April to 6.93 on 17 October (~9.7%), reserves have slipped from $3.13T to $3.07T, industrial production growth has eased from 6.8% to 5.9% y/y, and the PBOC’s fourth RRR cut of 2018 (announced 7 October) was followed by a >3% equity slide rather than a relief rally. Pence’s 4 October Hudson speech recast the dispute as whole-of-government containment, which raises the political and tech-sovereignty stakes beyond a tariff bargain. The case is not +0.8/+1.0 because merchandise exports have not collapsed, IP is still expanding, the 7.0 yuan line has been defended, and US-bound shipments were still being front-loaded into October. Action should stay at hold, not escalate: China has already matched Lists 1–2 and answered List 3 with 5–10% duties on ~$60B, covering most of the ~$130B US export base, so further tariff escalation has little ammunition and would make the threatened $267B more likely. A forced devaluation through 7 would risk 2015-style capital flight and confirm a currency-war charge. Concession or large purchase pledges are also wrong now: the 19 May joint statement was repudiated ten days later when the White House proceeded with 301, and after Pence’s speech any unrequited climbdown would look like yielding to a containment campaign. Hold preserves option value through the US midterms and the January rate cliff without firing remaining tools or selling industrial policy cheaply.
key_factors: US Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese goods; List 3 at 10% rises to 25% on 1 Jan 2019
Trump threat of an additional ~$267B would cover essentially all remaining China-to-US exports
CNY down ~10% toward the 7.0 line; FX reserves down ~$56B; fourth 2018 RRR cut and equity selloff
Tariff retaliation ammunition largely exhausted after the ~$60B List 3 response
May purchase-commitment truce collapsed when the US proceeded with 301
Pence 4 Oct speech frames a whole-of-government contest, raising the cost of unrequited concession

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
Trump directs USTR to finalize List 3: 10% tariffs on ~$200B of Chinese imports effective Sept 24, scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
China total reserves excl. gold from $3.129T (May) to $3.072T (Oct), about -$56B / -1.8%.
China industrial production index eased from 106.8 (May) to 105.9 (Oct).
Trump said he was prepared to immediately place tariffs on another $267 billion of imports if China takes retaliatory action against US farmers or other industries.
PBOC fourth RRR cut of 2018, 100bp effective Oct 15, to spur growth amid the trade dispute; PBOC said the cut would not create yuan depreciation pressure.
Pence: tariffs on $250B of Chinese goods with more possible unless a fair deal is made; accuses Beijing of a whole-of-government campaign against US interests.
Yuan slide of about 9% largely offset US duties; Beijing stabilized just above the psychological 7-per-dollar threshold; Wang Yi said China will not be blackmailed.
